title: Crowfoot Grass: How to Spot and Stop It in Your Rice Field
metaTitle: Crowfoot Grass in Rice Fields: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Crowfoot grass can cut rice yield by 10 to 75 percent. Learn to spot its bird's foot seed head early and keep it out of your rainfed palay.
excerpt: Crowfoot grass is a creeping grass weed with a seed head shaped like a bird's foot. In the Philippines it grows mostly in rainfed lowland rice fields, where the soil often dries out. This page shows how to spot it early, how much harm it does to palay and how to control it.

blocks.text:
Crowfoot grass (Dactyloctenium aegyptium) belongs to the grass family. Its local names include damong balang, bayakibok, krus krusan, sabong sabongan and tugot manok. Once you see its seed head, it is easy to remember, because it looks like a bird's foot or a small starfish. You will find it in rainfed lowland rice fields, where it does best on drier ground.

Most plants live for only one season, so it usually acts as an annual. Still, some plants live on and behave like a perennial. It spreads mainly by seed. Besides that, its lower stems creep, fork into pairs and root where they touch the soil. So a plant can sometimes spread by these runners, called stolons, as well as by seed.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about crowfoot grass
rows: Damong balang, bayakibok, krus krusan, sabong sabongan, tugot manok

blocks.text: This weed forms a low, spreading clump. Like other grasses, it has round, hollow stems with clear joints, or nodes. The lower stems creep along the ground, root at the joints and fork into two branches again and again. The flowering stems bend upward and then stand almost straight. At the top, short and thick spikes spread out from one point, like the toes of a bird's foot or the arms of a starfish.

items: Lower stems creep on the soil, root at the joints and fork into pairs.
Flowering stems rise at a slight angle and then stand nearly upright.
The seed head spreads out from one point like a bird's foot or a starfish.
Patches start on the higher, drier spots of rainfed fields where water does not stay.
Look alike tip: goosegrass also has finger spikes, but its spikes are longer and thinner than these short, thick ones.

blocks.text:
This weed is a C4 plant, so it grows fast in strong sun and heat. It also handles dry ground well. That makes it a real threat in rainfed fields when the rains pause. One plant can make up to 66,000 seeds, so a few plants left to mature can load the soil with seed for the next crop.

When it grows with palay, it can cut rice yield by 10 to 75 percent. Besides that, it serves as an alternate host of the tungro viruses and of rice bugs. In other words, both can stay alive on this weed while no rice is growing. Then they move back into your next crop.

items: Keep a steady layer of water in the field once your rice can take it. This grass prefers dry ground and struggles under flooding.
Level the field well so no high, dry spots remain, since patches usually start on those dry spots first.
Pull the plants before the seed heads open. One plant left to seed can drop thousands of seeds into your paddy.
When you pull it, lift the creeping stems too, because runner pieces left on wet soil can root again.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Grasses

If water and weeding cannot hold crowfoot grass down, choose an active ingredient that works on grasses at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Crowfoot Grass Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before the seed heads open, and clean the thresher and harvester before they enter the field.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [grass weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Crowfoot Grass

items.q: What do farmers call crowfoot grass in the Philippines?
items.a: Farmers use many local names for it. You may hear damong balang, bayakibok, krus krusan, sabong sabongan or tugot manok, depending on the region. Its scientific name is Dactyloctenium aegyptium. Some names cover more than one weed. For example, bayakibok is also a name for barnyard grass, so check for the bird's foot seed head to be sure.

items.q: How do I control crowfoot grass in a rice field?
items.a: Prevent it first. Use clean seed, level the field and keep water standing once the rice can take it, since this weed prefers dry soil. Next, hand weed early, before the seed heads open. If you still need a herbicide, pick one meant for grass weeds that suits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Can this weed spread diseases to my rice?
items.a: Yes, it can. It serves as an alternate host of the tungro viruses, so tungro can stay alive in your area while no rice is growing. It also shelters rice bugs between crops. So clear it from bunds, canals and fallow fields before you plant. That way you cut off the bridge between the weed and your next palay crop.
